consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on lamp oil symbolizing the Holy Spirit — His indwelling presence, sustaining grace, empowerment, and illumination — grounded chiefly in Zechariah 4, the tabernacle lamp texts (Ex 27:20-21), anointing passages (1 Sam 16:13; Acts 10:38), and the Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matt 25:1-13). Listed alternatives include genuine faith/grace, good works or charity, readiness/watchfulness as a non-allegorical plot device, and (as a minority reading) the Word of God/divine truth.
book_summary: The book identifies lamp oil as the commandment's truth and correction received and stored inwardly until they govern the life — proven, tested obedience laid up in the heart (the 'pressed fruit of the Spirit'), with light being that obedience made visible as an example. It explicitly flags the Holy Spirit reading as the 'commonly taught' view it departs from, citing Prov 6:23 ('the commandment is a lamp'), Ps 119:11, Prov 7:1-3, Jer 31:33, Ps 141:5 (reproof as 'excellent oil'), and 1 John 2:4.
consensus_core_identification: Lamp oil = the Holy Spirit (His presence, grace, and empowering that sustains the believer's light).
book_core_identification: Lamp oil = God's commandment/truth and correction internalized and stored as proven obedience that governs the life.
boundary_disagreement: The book reinterprets the same key lamp-oil passages (Ex 27:20; Zech 4; Matt 25:3-9) but assigns them a different referent. Where the consensus reads the oil as the Spirit Himself, the book reads it as internalized commandment and proven obedience — the Spirit's product, not the Spirit. In Matthew 25 this reclassifies what the foolish virgins lack: not the indwelling Spirit but stored, tested obedience to received truth and correction.
material_contradiction: The consensus identifies the oil as the Spirit (the divine source); the book identifies it as stored obedience to commandment/truth (a human-side, worked-in product), and its own common-view note explicitly sets its reading against the 'commonly taught: the Holy Spirit' identification. The phrase 'pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience' acknowledges causal derivation from the Spirit while denying that the oil IS the Spirit — a source/product distinction that the rubric treats as different referents. Accepting the book requires replacing the consensus identification, not merely tightening it.
rationale: Every blind response makes the Holy Spirit the primary meaning. The book displaces that identification with internalized commandment/truth stored as proven obedience, and it self-consciously marks the Spirit reading as the common view it corrects. Its reading partially resembles two listed alternatives — the minority 'Word of God/divine truth' reading (Prov 6:23; Ps 119:105) and the 'good works/obedience' reading — so it is not NOVEL; a recognizable interpretive lineage exists. But because the book's core replaces the consensus's central referent rather than refining its boundary (obedience produced by the Spirit is not the Spirit), the correct verdict is DIVERGENT. The distinctive fusion (truth + reproof received, laid up, and proven in obedience; light = visible obedience per Matt 5:16) is a specific synthesis not centrally represented in any consensus response.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED or even near-MATCH-with-alternative: the book's reading combines the listed 'Word of God/truth' and 'good works/obedience' alternatives, and its 'fruit of the Spirit' language keeps the Spirit in the causal chain, so it might be seen as a precision of the broad Spirit-and-grace category rather than a replacement. However, the alternatives were minority/secondary readings, the consensus core across all four responses is the Spirit Himself, and the book's own contrast note shows it intends replacement of that core, not refinement.
